header:
Date: 2025-08-20
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nambiar (Redwood SE), Devon Park (Redwood SRE), Maya Singh (Redwood Product), Jordan Patel (Nexus ML), Samira Lopez (Nexus Infra), Liam O'Reilly (Nexus Security), Hana Kim (Nexus Data)
summary: Technical deep dive focusing on GPU runtime profiling for multi-tenant inference: kernel selection heuristics, CUDA graph micro-batching, eviction-aware KV cache strategies, and side-by-side TRT-LLM vs vLLM behavior. Customer provided production-like traffic patterns and is concerned about tail latency and multi-tenant fragmentation on shared hardware. Agreed next steps to run controlled benchmarks and a short on-prem smoke test.
topics: KV cache eviction policies and effect on latency
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We'll dive straight into the perf bits — Priya and Devon will drive the kernel and infra topics. Jordan, Samira, if you want to interrupt with your live traces that'd be great.
[00:20] Jordan Patel: Yep, thanks. We sent a heatmap earlier — mostly short chatty prompts, 8-64 tokens usually but spikes to 1024 during long-form generation.
[00:32] Priya Nambiar: Got it, that distribution matters a lot for kernel pathing and KV cache hits. Quick agenda: kernel selection heuristics -> CUDA graphs and micrograph batching -> eviction-aware cache policies -> tensor-quant tradeoffs -> on-prem considerations.
[00:47] Samira Lopez: Our main ask is keeping p95 below 220ms for the 13B tail segments; we'll tolerate higher cost but can't blow SLA.
[00:59] Devon Park: Important to note multi-tenant fragmentation — if we pack many small requests the allocator will fragment GPU memory unless we use pinned pooling + deferred free.
[01:12] Hana Kim: Quick question, is Redwood using persistent CUDA graphs per model shard or per inference session? We saw graphs sometimes recompiled causing stalls.
[01:28] Priya Nambiar: We prefer persistent graphs keyed by (model-version, dtype, sequence_bucket). But there's a trade: graphs for every sequence length yields fast runs but high memory/graph overhead. We often use a small set of dynamic-shape graphs and fallback kernels.
[01:48] Liam O'Reilly: From security POV, on-prem means we can't just pull container images from public registries — we need signed artifacts and control plane isolation. We'll review the whitepaper you share.
[02:01] Alex Chen: Noted. Back to kernel choice: we saw best perf when attention kernels were fused and run with 128-token tiling for 13B. Priya, can you show the micro-bench notes?
[02:12] Priya Nambiar: Sure. Slide note: fused attention + rotary precompute moved from compute-bound to memory-bound for 13B, improving throughput by ~18% on our 80GB A100 tests. But with 4-bit quant, kernel paths differ: some fused kernels aren't compatible with specific int4 packing layouts, so we fall back to a different compute path.
[02:36] Jordan Patel: That's the kind of thing we hit — quantization sometimes increases latency because fallback kernels are unoptimized. In our tests with post-training quant we saw p95 jump.
[02:50] Priya Nambiar: Exactly — warmup strategy fix: run a tiny calibration pass to populate KV caches and initialize CUDA graphs with the expected shapes before accepting production traffic. That avoids first-request stalls.
[03:06] Samira Lopez: For the KV cache eviction strategy — can you explain eviction-aware batching? We use LRU today and it thrashes when many short sessions exist.
[03:18] Priya Nambiar: Eviction-aware batching aims to group requests that will reuse KV cache prefixes together. Practically we tag sessions with conversation-id hash, schedule those close in time, and avoid packing unrelated sessions into the same micro-batch if that will cause cache churn. This decreases cold-KV misses.
[03:39] Jordan Patel: But doesn't grouping by conversation add scheduling latency? Our traffic is bursty.
[03:45] Priya Nambiar: Slightly yes, but we use a hybrid: when latency SLO is tight we allow dynamic batching up to small batch size; when throughput is higher we use affinity-based micro-batches for cache locality. The tuning knob is a per-route policy.
[04:01] Devon Park: Also memory fragmentation is critical. We observed that enabling a deferred free queue and reusing GPU allocators for KV cache slices reduces fragmentation by ~40% in a mixed workload.
[04:15] Hana Kim: How do CUDA graphs interact with micro-batches? If we persist graphs keyed to batch size, many distinct batch sizes create many graphs.
[04:26] Priya Nambiar: We use micrograph composition: a base graph for single-token step and a loop-unrolled graph for common small-batch sizes. For uncommon sizes we fall back to JIT path. The composition reduces total graph count while keeping hot-path fast.
[04:44] Jordan Patel: For TRT-LLM vs vLLM, which one is more amiable to micrograph tactics? We've tried both and results varied.
[04:53] Priya Nambiar: TRT-LLM often benefits from ahead-of-time kernel optimizations and can bake a lot into the graph — so micrographs shine. vLLM's dynamic engine is better for highly varying shapes but sometimes pays overhead per call. Benchmarks show TRT-LLM with static-ish traffic is superior in p50/p95 but vulnerable to shape variability.
[05:14] Alex Chen: We ran a quick 13B matrix: TRT-LLM p95 195ms for 256-token bucket on A100, vLLM p95 240ms but with more graceful degradation at odd shapes. Those numbers will be in the sheet.
[05:28] Samira Lopez: We also care about quantization. 8-bit vs 4-bit — what's your recommendation?
[05:35] Priya Nambiar: 8-bit usually gives good latency and simpler kernels. 4-bit can reduce memory and allow bigger batch, but brings packing/unpacking cost and often forces kernel fallbacks. If you need to double concurrency, 4-bit is attractive, but expect more engineering to maintain fused fast paths.
[05:53] Jordan Patel: Any notes on attention kernel fusing when using rotary embeddings? We saw numeric deviations in some fused kernels.
[06:02] Priya Nambiar: Fused kernels must carefully implement rotary rotations; small FP errors are expected in lower precision. We have QA thresholds and rollback flags to drop to reference kernel if deltas exceed threshold. We'll share eval scripts.
[06:20] Hana Kim: Does Redwood support top-K reranking inside the graph so we avoid device-host-device transfers?
[06:28] Devon Park: Yes, we recommend doing top-k on device; transfer only final tokens. That avoids PCIe roundtrips and reduces tail latency.
[06:36] Jordan Patel: About compilation times — TRT-LLM builds are longer, sometimes minutes. That impacts deploys. How do you manage rollout?
[06:46] Priya Nambiar: Build artifacts are cached in our artifact store. We do canary rollouts with dual serving for a while. For private deploys we also provide prebuilt signed images if compilation isn't allowed on prem.
[07:01] Liam O'Reilly: Security question — signed artifact is fine. For on-prem inference we also need KMS integration for model keys and isolated telemetry. Any constraints?
[07:12] Alex Chen: We integrate with customer KMS/HSM and support pull-only images, no external egress. We'll share the private-deploy checklist.
[07:22] Priya Nambiar: Back to perf: one interesting micro-optimization — reduce padding by bucketing sequences into 2-3 size buckets and using per-bucket CUDA graphs with dynamic stride. This saves wasted compute.
[07:37] Jordan Patel: That matches our intuition. However, with many buckets scheduler becomes complex.
[07:42] Priya Nambiar: We capped at three buckets for most of our production workloads — short (<=64), medium (65-256), long (>256). Combined with eviction-aware affinity, it's a good tradeoff.
[07:55] Samira Lopez: How about multi-GPU scaling and NCCL issues? We saw interconnect contention sometimes worsens tail latency.
[08:04] Devon Park: For synchronous multi-GPU lower batch sizes can be problematic. We prototype pipeline parallel or tensor-sliced serving for large models. Also, prefer NVLink-rich topology for serving and avoid cross-node NCCL for latency-sensitive routes.
[08:20] Hana Kim: Any CPU-side bottlenecks? We noticed kernel launch overheads and host-to-device pinning issues.
[08:28] Priya Nambiar: Use pinned host buffers and prefetching. Also consolidate small memcpy into a single larger one where possible. For kernel launches we aggregate operations in the CUDA graph to reduce launch overhead.
[08:41] Jordan Patel: Can we see an example micro-batch policy?
[08:45] Priya Nambiar: Sure — example: route A (chat): max_latency 200ms, max_micro_batch 8, affinity window 500ms, bucket_policy [64,256,1024], warmup 3 requests. We'll drop that into the shared sheet.
[08:59] Alex Chen: Quick note on observability — metrics to watch: per-shard KV hit rate, graph compile rate, deferred-free backlog, host->device memcpy ms, kernel occupancy.
[09:12] Samira Lopez: Good. On the On-Prem smoke test — we want Redwood to exercise both TRT and vLLM flavors in our lab. We'll provide a node with 4xA100.
[09:22] Devon Park: Perfect; we'll need SSH and signed sigs to push images. We'll run TRT-LLM with dynamic shape buckets and vLLM with same sequence distribution. Expect 6-8h of bench runs.
[09:34] Jordan Patel: Please include a run that simulates cold-starts: KV cache emptied and traffic ramp from 0 to full QPS.
[09:41] Priya Nambiar: Agreed. We'll include cold-start traces and a warm-run after 30 minutes.
[09:47] Hana Kim: Anything about CUDA Graph persistent memory leaks? We've seen leaks after many graph replays.
[09:53] Devon Park: We instrument with graph refcounts and run periodic GC cycles during low traffic windows. Also set a hard cap on graph cache size to avoid unbounded growth.
[10:03] Jordan Patel: For the benchmark spreadsheet — do you have a column for quantization pack format so we can match ours?
[10:09] Priya Nambiar: Yes, we'll include pack format, kernel variant, compute cap, and a reproducible run command. The benchmark link will be in the follow-up.
[10:18] Alex Chen: Let's surface a couple risks: TRT-LLM's build fragility for some custom ops, and vLLM's occasional per-request overhead on very small tokens. We mitigate with canary and routing policies.
[10:32] Samira Lopez: For routing, can Redwood route to a cheaper model for non-critical journeys?
[10:36] Maya Singh: Yes, we can set routing rules by route: e.g., 'summary' only uses 7B quantized; 'secure' route pins to private 13B. We'll include recommended policies.
[10:49] Jordan Patel: One more curious point — do you use CUDA Graphs for attention KV updates or only for token generation?
[10:56] Priya Nambiar: Both. We compose graphs such that KV update is a node in the graph; that allows the entire step to be replayed with single launch. It helps reduce per-token overhead.
[11:09] Alex Chen: Alright we'll wrap with concrete next steps. Any final quick questions?
[11:14] Liam O'Reilly: Please include required compliance artifacts for private deploy.
[11:18] Alex Chen: We'll send SOC2 + architecture notes. Thanks all.
[57:00] Alex Chen: Final recap — Redwood runs matrix, Nexus shares traces, schedule on-prem smoke test, share benchmark link and security whitepaper. Thanks everyone.
[58:00] Meeting ends.
